messages.author: 13655805b578fc86
messages.subject: Problem with autoc
parts:
I have a WAV file which contains three transient waveforms which have
a high harmonic content. The harmonics are very visible in a
spectrogram. I am trying to use autoc to detect the waveforms and
calculate the fundamental frequency of each. Unfortunately, autoc
isn't returning the results I want. When I use the parameter
"fmax=500", it appears that autoc is returning all fundamental
frequency estimates above 1000 Hz, not equal to or lower than 500 Hz
as I expect. Is this a bug, or do I misunderstand something? Thanks
in advance for your help.

I have posted my R script, graphical results, and the WAV file at
http://guaminsects.net/anr/content/problem-autoc

Thanks in advance for your help.

- Aubrey

messages.author: de80047cbc18c87e
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Problem with autoc
parts:
Hi,

The main problem with your sound is that it is very noisy. Whatever the
parameters you use, it will always be very difficult to catch the
fundamental frequency.

You should first isolate the buz you would like to analyse. Then try to
remove as much as noise as possible with fir(). Eventually, it seems
that using the function fund() instead of autoc() gives better results.
Here is an example:

> s <- readWave("05-02_9_2_example.wav")
> f <- s...@samp.rate
> s1 <- cutw(s, from=9.5, to=9.8)
> s1F <- fir(s1, f, from=300)
> fund <- fund(s1F, f, ovlp=75, fmax=500, plot=FALSE)
> spectro(s1F, f, collevels=seq(-84,0, 1), scale=FALSE, ovlp=75)
> points(fund, pch=20)

Another solution could be to use a FFT. You compute a spectrum right in
the middle of you sound of interest and then you get the peaks values
with fpeaks(). You just need then to compute the difference between two
successive peaks to get an estimation of the fundamental:

> res <- spec(s1F, f, at=0.12)
> res2 <- fpeaks(res, amp=c(0.01,0.01))
> res2[2,1]-res2[1,1]
freq
0.1875

version and tried to install it. It failed again, it seems that the

messages.author: de80047cbc18c87e
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Problems postscript files
parts:
Hi,

Saving a spectrogram in a vectorial format (.ps, .eps or pdf) is not a
great idea. A spectrogram is usually made of thousand points. This
generates huge vectorial files, sometimes difficult to open with a viewer.

You should choose a bitmapped image format instead (.bmp, .jpeg, .png or
.tiff).

Actually, the best thing to do seems to use the .png format employs
lossless data compression.

Usually the following parameters produce a nice graph:

png("myspectro.png", width=1200, height=1200, point=24)
data(tico)
spectro(tico, f=22050)
dev.off()

Best

Jerome

messages.author: acc632d9ccc1c73a
messages.subject: Re: Temporal parameters
parts:
Hi Tomi,

Sorry for the delay.
A solution for the buzzing part of your cicada song is to try to
analyse the amplitude modulation. You can do that with the function
ama().

Try this:

# reading the file
a <- readWave("DAT-Kreta01-36-B14.wav")
# selection of the buzzing part
buzz <- cutw(a, from=0.075, to=1.6)
# amplitude modulation analysis
res <- ama(buzz, f=48000, plot=FALSE)
# peak search
fpeaks(res)

On the resulting graph you see:
o a peak at ~ 840 Hz that corresponds to a slow amplitude modulation,
ie. the repetition rate of your group of pulses.
o a peak at ~ 1500 Hz that corresponds to a fast amplitude modulation,
ie. the repetition rate of your pulses.

HTH

Jerome

messages.subject: Compiling Seewave in R version 2.11.1
parts:
Hi Jerome and others,
Has Seewave been tested in R 2.11.1 yet? After upgrading R to version
2.11.1 and calling seewave I was prompted to re-install the package. The
problem now is that some of its modules do not compile successfully in
2.11.1.

Thanks,
Vincent
